review:
The "Mixed" review status is down to a game-breaking bug that emerged shortly after launch; to the developers' credit, it was fixed very quickly (but was rather upsetting while it lasted). I don't think it's justified any more, but it was at the time. Don't let it dissuade you anymore!

As for my thoughts on this game; it's fantastic. It's a 4X game that focuses heavily on your chosen faction's story, and how it progresses as time goes on. You get to make real, meaningful choice that continue a well-written plot.
If that's not your thing, this is still a totally brilliant turn-based strategy game. I'd definitely recommend it to anyone, especially if they enjoyed the first Endless Space.

This is the first Steam review I've done, and I'm only doing it because Endless Space 2 is really that fun to me. Lately, it feels like the trend of developers seems to be all about the profits and less about the true enjoyment of the game. As Amplitude Studios seems to be one of the few exceptions to that trend, I felt I owed it to them to leave a review.

About the game:
I stumbled on Endless Space 2 out of the blue several months ago and decided to give it a shot as it was only $40 and seemed interesting enough. There are very few games that I truly feel have paid off as much as this one has for me. I find the game to have a great deal of depth and replayability. I have a huge amount of hours on this game and find myself still discovering new features and fun combinations (regarding things like research, expansion methods, etc.) I hadn't thought of before. Moreover, the game has an amazing soundtrack that really adds to the overall atmosphere and feel of the game.

About the developers:
Since I have been playing, the developers have released two big (free) updates and have a new big (free) update coming tomorrow. I recently started to follow the game's website (Games2Gether) and noticed a lot of the changes they have implemented come directly from player feedback, which I feel is very rare now days. If you don't believe me, checkout the "Trending Ideas" section of the website and you'll find various ideas that players have suggested with the status of "Implemented" tagged to them by Devs.

TL;DR: Great game, great atmosphere, great replayability, great devs. Highly recommend.

A big fan of Endless Space and -Legend, I bought ES2 as soon as it was available. Though while I appreciate the community-guided production setup run by Amplitude, early access is not for me. So I did not launch the game until public release.

One week later, 49 hours in (buh-bye vacation), I come up for air - to see the sun, greet my family, and write this review.

I guess I'll just start enumerating impressions and see where that goes:
1: ES2 does not break what I enjoyed in ES1.
2: The lessons learned in Legend are well applied to ES2 - not directly copied, but properly adapted. Heroes, quests, challenges, politics. I don't know that the adaptations would work well in Legends, but they work really well here.
3: Expanding the early game of ES1 in ES2 has worked really well. Exploration is interesting and tie-in with quests and challenges works.
4: I have a hard time dealing with foes gunning for economic victory, so I have resolved to exclude that victory condition from my default skirmish game and not play against the Lumeris faction, given that it is explicitly designed for that win.
5: Building on the battles of ES1 works well, but I have had a couple of sessions where the AI would just not realise the ineffectiveness of their 100% close range designs, making them easily exploitable.
6: Generally the level of polish on ES2 is off the charts. ES1 and Legend were great in this regard, but ES2 dials it to 11.
7: Stability-wise I have had no major issues there is the occasional missing localisation or odd inaccessible node, but that's about it. My play setup is running off a Win7 machine, streaming to a mac mini via in-home streaming, controlled via the steam controller.

So in short: Absolutely amazing experience - exactly what I hoped it would be. That said, I do have a library category titled "Danger, Will Robinson!" for a reason.

I came to this game as a lover of civilizations 5.  there was a bit of a learning curve, but once i figured out how to navigate the tech circle as opposed to civ's tech tree i came to realize endless space is a far more interesting game than Civ.  Endless space 2 is loaded with lore of a fantastic galaxy. every play-through I end up reading something new that intrigues me, or just makes me laugh.  

The civilizations available to play in ES2 play quite differently from each other, much more than in civ 5 where each civ only differs by an ability, a building, and a unit.  The fact that human players and AI can not just work together, but win together, makes for exciting strategies and game play you would never see in Civ 5.  The Vaulters with their portals (which are open to them AND their allies) are a great example of this.  

Diplomacy feels much more reasonable in ES2 when compared to Civ 5 as well (Unless you have the misfortune of being neighbors with the Cravers).  I have been saved countless times by my AI allies when interlopers find their way past my front line fleets.  In Civ 5 i would be surprised if the AI units ever figured out how to navigate past lakes or ocean to even get into my land to help or destroy me.  If you treat your AI allies well in ES2 often they well return the favor. In Civ they just demand you give them your marble because youre "friends" in name only.
Quests in ES2 open the game to lore and gameplay possibilities often unique to each empire.  It accomplishes with grace what Civ's Beyond Earth installment tried and failed to do.  The quests for the most part are optional, and if you dont care about missing an opportunity for a small bonus reward you don't have to bother with them and can focus on galactic domination if you so desire.  
I feel like i could write an entire essay about why I like Endless space 2 but I am now bored of typing and want to get back to culling the disgusting vine spread of the Unfallen from the center of my galaxy with the help of my beautiful best friend and ally, Horatio.
Buy this game.

First of all. Im not a very good turn based strategy player, and i find  this genre really time consuming, which was a problem for me when playing civilisation, but this game really got my attention. I love this game. 
To sum it up. It is civilisation/ stellaris with a space setting with interesting additions. 

You play as one of nine Empires. That might not sound like a lot but damn those Empires are really really amazing. Compared to civ where all you get is a new unit or building and a rather small trait that is helping in game a bit the civs in this game are all like playing a different game. They all have very unique mechanics like connecting new systems with vines or even not settling in systems at all but rather living in ships able to fly from one system to another. Also every Empire comes with a unique background and quests ingame that develop a unique story for all of them. It can be ignored entirely when you not like  it  but the ones i read were quite interesting. Nothing big though. 

Gameplay is classic turn based strategy gameplay. Build up your systems, manage your different ressources and military and expand to new systems to win through money generation, science, by building unique buildings or of course by expanding and deleting each and every other empire trying to conquer the galaxy.

Combat is split in two parts. Space combat and invasions. You build ships and equip them with different weapons or utility mods and staff. Then you can fight the enemy fleets and if you want to you can watch an amazing sequence of the fleets shootin each other with lasers or rockets it looks great but more about that later. Also there is a tactics system where you can  select differnt strategies your ships are going to use in battle.  
The invasions are less spectacular and just use the troops on your ship to conquer planets or destroy them from other empires. They also have a tiny degree of decisionmaking that is taking place in the form of choosing the type of ground units you want to use and how they are going to  fight but much less complex than the ship to ship combat with a lot less interesting animations if you can call them that. 
Other systems in game are a diplomacy system, minor civilisations to take over by different means, multiplayer quests ingame to build something or reach a goal before your enemys do, unique events that can appear affecting you both positive or negative and differnt populations that you can aquire and manage  granting different effects on differnt planets that you can manage, All those systems can easily be ignored if you choose so and you can still play the game and have fun but they will make your games more effective and desicion heavy.

For me the biggest selling point of this game though overshadowing everything else is the visuals. This game is gorgeous, Everything. The interface the universe the ship to ship combat its so great to look at and just lean back and relax while pressing that end turn button over and over again. All paired with an amazing soundtrack in the  background that made me hum along over and over again and changes quite a bit from empire to empire. 

So as a casual player who played some games vs the computer on normal difficulty i can really recommend this game.
If you are looking for a turn based game to enjoy your time try it maybe you will enjoy it as much as i did.
People looking to play this seriously in competitive manner i cant really relate to. I cant tell how easy or hard this game is on higher difficulties and how balanced and fair the civs are. Also i have no clue if there are multiplayer games that you can join in without having a group of friends playing with. All i can say is that the normal ai wasnt to ahrd to beat for me no matter which win condition i was going for. Also there are some things to read into like the tech tree and the market and so on but after a bit of reading and playing i got the hang of it enough to play the game and feel like i know what im doing. Its a bit of stuff to get into but its manageble as a casual player.

PROS
-Immersive soundtrack, cinematography, and dialogue.  
-Intuitive, easy to use interface.  
-Unique VERY interesting races which each have vastly different play styles.  The standard humans breed in the standard fashion (you know the details), while the bio-engineered Cravers consume planets, the greedy Lumeris buy planets/influence, the religious zealot Vodyani leech away other races, and the genetically obsessed Horatio(s) graft whole sub-species into their own.  This produces significant replay value by varying the races and the shape/constituents of the galaxy.  Hence the >300 hours total.    
-Multi-layer complexity: the game is very much a complex 4x space opera, but the learning curve is appropriately gradual.  The nuances are interesting and fun, but not critically imperative.  
-Pirates: With the most recent patch the early game pirates are surprisingly strong (likely attenuated in a future patch).  This makes for an early game challenge rather than an outright planet grab.
-Heros: Heros are interesting, adaptable, and helpful.  You will find yourself getting attached to them.
-The developers at Amplitude Studios definitely are committed to being free DLC and improvements, much appreciated.

CONS
-Despite the talk of ranges and ship classes, combat really comes down to who has the highest number of advanced ships in each engagement.  There is some variation; aka missiles work best a Long, compared to short burst projectiles which are best at Short.  But I find myself rarely changing my tactics in any meaningful way.  It is also impossible to intervene once a battle starts.  I find myself rarely watching battles.
-Heros: Heroes have the same basic starship hull from beginning to end.  Not a big deal, but definitely a place for some diversity.
-Quests: The quests are interesting and deep, but few.  A few dozen more (with maybe more varied rewards) would liven up the game play.
-AI: The AI is generally hostile to you, which I find slightly monotone.  Variability would be nice in this area as well.  
-After a certain point the game is difficult to lose (Yes, to the chorus of haters, I have continually increased the difficulty).  The game lacks existential obstacles which need negotiated; such as the Black Death or the Mongol Invasion in the Total War series.  As long as you keep your planets happy and have the biggest/most advanced fleet then you will win.
-Most importantly (imho), despite the VERY diverse, interesting races...they all share the same tech tree, same weapons and roughly the same warship hulls (small, medium, large, etc).   Why would a race of Ent-creatures (the Unfallen) use weapons/ships/tactics of a race that is not from their dimension (the Riftborn).  In my humble opinion, this is a failure of vision on behalf of the game designers. Older games, such as Conquest: Frontier Wars, made each race radically different in offensive capabilities, armaments, hull design, etc.  The Vodyani should have sprawling carriers crewed with their subjected races, the United Empire should have massive battleships, and the Cravers should have suicidally under-shielded glass cannons and focus on boarding parties.  Maybe the Unfallen can throw pine cones.

TL;DR: An immersive, streamlined 4x space opera well worth the price tag.  The diverse races provide significant replayability.

--- original review follows ---

The good: See the other reviews. I concur with them that this is an excellent title in the making. I am recommending this game, but with some caveats for all you 4X fans who are thinking about picking this game up on release day, so read on before spending your money. 

The problematic: There are still some game-killing bugs that occur when you push the engine. Try playing for an exclusive Supremacy Victory on any of the largest map sizes with the game speed on 'endless' and before you finish conquering half of the galaxy you'll be unhappily familiar with all of these issues. I did manage to make it as far as turn 687 on my latest attempt which is a minor miracle.

Amplitude has an excellent track record of solid patching and supporting games for years after they launch, so I am confident these issues will be resolved, if not with the promised 'miracle patch' at release, within a matter of months afterwards. That's the only reason I'm still recommending this game in its current state. If you want to enjoy this game right now, stick to fast paced games in small galaxies against a limited number of factions. That'll give you the best chance to avoid the errors.

Now, let's talk issues...

1. The engine has an unfortunate tendency to lose track of ships internally. If this happens, somewhere on the map, after a battle, will sit a single hero ship that is frozen in place with no stats (all are set to zero). The trigger for this seems to be when a fleet attempts to retreat, but has no place to go, and is therefore eliminated. The hero ship for that fleet will sometimes reappear the next turn and then freeze the turn after that in this broken state. The next time the game engine attempts to interact with this ship, it will hang. This can result in saves made with such a ship present that will get stuck on infinite loading. If a battle is attempted against this ship, it will never complete and hang indefinitely. Ending your turn may result in getting stuck in a 'pending' state indefinitely. I've only had this happen to AI controlled ships, never player controlled. (edit: fixed in release, no more hangs)

2. The build queues can't handle a serious load. By the time you have 40+ systems under your control and start to terraform planets, the queues on some systems will bug out, leaving that solar system in an unusable state. IF this happens, you can work around it by 'evacuating' the bugged system, and then recolonizing it again (remember to send your populations to other planets first). The trigger for this bug seems to be a large number of items in the queues of multiple star systems, and/or a large number of bought out items in a single system queue. In particular, buying out terraforming and colonization events seem to be the worst triggers, I've never seen this bug happen on any other items, even if buying out all non-planetary constructions on an already-bugged queue. It's directly related to planetary build items somehow. Best to let colonization, terraforming, and planet specialization items build without buying them out, or stick to buying out just one or two items on a single system at a time. That seems to help work around the error, though it isn't a foolproof trick. (Edit: fixed in release, abused queues relentlessly without trouble)

3. Ungodly long wait times for a turn to complete in busy games. I'm not sure this is a 'bug' or just a lack of optimization, but the larger the map, the more ships, the more empires fighting, the longer turns take to complete, sometimes in excess of five minutes. Something really needs to be done to cut this time down. (edit: unbelievably fixed, turns take like five seconds now no matter the size)

4. Whatever algorithm draws the empire borders based on influence is still a bit screwy. Borders will occasionally fragment in very strange ways that make no sense, particularly on long games over large influence areas. These borders will even redraw themselves differently on reloading the same save games. This is more of an annoyance than a serious gameplay issue. (edit: not sure if fixed but hasn't made a reappearance yet)

5. There's work to be done balancing the economics. All the right bells and whistles are there, but when you have a single star system producing in excess of 30K of a resource (when you are only mining tens of units and can only store 999 of them) something about the trade routes and trading companies production bonuses is a bit broken. It's trivial to end up being able to sell multiple stacks of 999 resources *per turn* on the market and rake in millions of dust *per turn* in addition to your normal income. (edit: this has been fixed completely in release version)

6. Some of the AIs are just plain idiots. Cravers, Horatio, and Sophons always seem to peak at a low/mid tier tech level (if they are lucky) and then get steamrolled effortlessly by anyone. Meanwhile the Lumeris and Riftborn tend to steamroll everything in their path and provide a good challenge to the player. The AI for certain factions definitely need some polish. (edit: release version is much improved, AI is kicking my ass again)

Those are the only issues that bother me. Sure, there are other things we'd all like to see (a lot more quests, more planet variety, more espionage-related activities, etc) but all of those issues will be addressed by modders eventually if Amplitude doesn't do it themselves. I'm not worried so much about content as about the current health of the engine. If these issues are present on launch day the company could get a bit of a black eye, so I'm hoping that miracle patch lives up to its name.

If working around these issues bothers you, then you might want to wait until after Amplitude patches them to buy this game. (Edit: Or perhaps just trust that they deliver on their promises unlike most studios today. Excellent job, guys.)

One good mark I will add that not enough people talk about: modding capability. This game is pure XML, which makes it more easily and thoroughly moddable than Skyrim or XCOM. The mods for the original Endless Space were pretty good, the mods for this are likely to be more epic than Requiem or Long War. That's a few years down the road, however. I just think it's worth pointing out the possibilities. They've given people a very large, full featured engine to build around and that's laudable.

Endless Space II is a game you happily play through once per faction or so but probably not much more. It is really enjoyable at first, but its relative lack of replayability is a major downside.

GOOD:
-The look and feel puts a lot of other turn-based strategy games to shame. The music is good. The writing is good. And with a couple notable exceptions, the graphics are great. The hand-painted art panels compare well to non-digital tabletop games. And the strategic map is attractive, informative, even dynamic. The planets orbit their stars and moons orbit their planets.
-There is a good amount of detail to manage, no micromanagement. The star system is the basic unit of galactic development, rather than individual planets. Still, individual planets each have their own properties that contribute to their systems.
-Each race or faction is truly unique with its own story and often a significant modification to the game mechanics, not just a little bonus here and there, like other games.
-Exploration ships launch expeditions on planetside “curiosities” as well as launch probes into deep space to discover unknown systems. The rewards gained from searching goodie huts are just about right.
-Technology is laid out in concentric circles, leaving a lot of freedom to prioritize and differentiate. It always feels like any one technology is pretty achievable but getting all the techs is nearly impossible.
-There is a good balance between moving along established “star lanes” and (later) free movement of ships.
-Strategy really matters in a satisfying way. There are meaningful long-term consequences for turn-by-turn decisions.

MIXED:
-Fleet battles are non-tactical. Players do not control ships at all during combat, but rather choose from a list of predefined battle tactics that typically revolve around staying in optimal weapons range or boosting the right type of defense. Space battles are shown in cinematic quality, but most players will probably not watch them much.
-Population management is clearly intended, as certain races have bonuses on certain types of planets. However, population movement between systems is so slow as to frustrate any thorough attempt to manage this aspect of the empire.
-Population and food movement, as well as trade, are handled automatically, but it would be nice if the player could upgrade the merchant fleet to make it faster, more resistant to blockade.
-The politics mechanic is interesting but not really powerful enough to matter much. Some laws become potent in certain situations, but most are pretty so-so. Anarchy has very little effect. Ultimately the elections become an almost meaningless distraction.
-Heroes are a big part of the Endless franchise, and choosing their promotions as they level up is both enjoyable and strategic. However, while heroes level up quickly governing systems, they barely level up at all as fleet admirals.
-Quests are good at first but get very repetitive later. Many quests are easy, but some are too difficult. The late-game Academy questline seems especially pointless, strategically speaking, because it requires such a huge investment of time and resources (i.e. heroes).
-The AI is decent--at least not terrible--but slow.

BAD:
-Lack of replayability is a huge issue. There should be an optional random quest generator.
-Ship movement is not user-friendly. It is sometimes hard to select a fleet and choose its destination. Worse, the pathfinding for fleet movements gives little control to the player. Fleets will often walk straight into unnecessary conflict, even when other paths are theoretically available.
-From a technical standpoint, the game is unreasonably slow and resource-hungry. This seems to be mostly for the sake of AI processing.
-Economic victory is a little too easy to achieve accidentally.
-Ground battle animations and fleet representations on the strategic map view are the two notable exceptions to the otherwise excellent graphics.
-Outpost growth predictions are not accurate.
-Certain aspects of the game are unnecessarily opaque, such as how combat is resolved, what happens to leftover production and research points, and how ship experience works.

I want to like this game. The graphics are beautiful, the sound design is great, the writing is great, and it has many great ideas. 

But dear God, the game design is atrocious. In no particular order:

- Alliances give each member total power over all diplomacy, for all members. So if you're allied with [Ally A], and fighting against [Enemy B], you could be on the verge of capturing a critical planet and your "ally" will just randomly sign a peace treaty on behalf of both of you. You don't get to refuse, or veto, or anything. This makes fighting wars with allies pointless.

- Cultural takeover of neutral planets can occur. Ok. But this is instant, with no counter-play, with the most insanely braindead mechanics. E.g. you've just invaded and captured [Planet A]. This planet instantly loses all its cultural power because it's under a new owner (you). So a nearby neutral planet now smothers it with cultural power, and instantly converts it on the next turn. Your invasion forces haven't even left the planet yet, and it's magically decided to hand itself over to a third power. You're forced to declare war on all nearby neutral powers as a result.

- Planets can only be seiged effectively with specialist ship components. The AI never builds these components, so the AI is incapable of seiging properly defended planets. It makes the game trivially easy.

- The map generator is abysmal. An "8 arm galaxy" with 8 players chooses to put multiple players on the same arm, and leave some arms completely empty. This is wildly unbalanced. Maps in general are incredibly easy because they all consist of nothing but choke points where the player can concentrate everything into a single frontline planet. Regardless of how you play with the options, it's impossible to create a map with wide fronts, or put the player in the middle of a dense network of systems, or to have any meaningful variety. Even if you fill a galaxy with many different races, you'll be stuck fighting the same one for most of the game because the maps are so constrictive, and there's nothing to incentivise long distance expeditions. Most starts will put you very near an edge, with only one neighbour, and only one channel for them to reach you. It's braindead levels of easy. You're forced to reload the generator 10-20 times just to get somewhere near the middle, and even then, you'll still only have 2 or 3 enemies.

- The AI often refuses to attack the player even when it has very hostile relations and vastly superior strength. In general the AI is incredibly passive.

- The ships need to be designed, with different components giving different buffs. This is awesome! But the AI is incapable of designing good ships, and for some baffling reason the game designers didn't just upload a series of good templates for the AI to follow.

- The number of systems you can colonise is very limited. Ok, fair enough. But there's no way to control uncolonised systems, which is mind-bogglingly stupid because it means you end up getting an empire with either: (a) passage blocked from one half to the other because the AI colonised the barren rock in the middle, or (b) you spend one of your precious colonisation slots to occupy the otherwise worthless rock. Having systems within your borders doesn't prevent colonisation. The Hissho have mechanics for permanently mining uncolonised systems but it's pointless/broken because the AI just colonises them, even if they're the Hissho's allies.

There's so many more. The game is riddled with baffling decisions that just render it a frustrating experience.

Worth getting!

If you ignore the gameplay and just appreciate it for its visuals,

However, the game’s flaws are very obvious.

Within the first 2–10 hours, you’ll discover its charm,
filled with great curiosity and expectation,
and you’ll very likely become obsessed with it.

TLDR review: As much as I wanted to love it, I didn't. Clean, beautiful, elegant, and so boring that clicking the end turn button feels like a never ending chore. I kept forcing myself to play this game to see if I was missing something or give it a chance to grow on me but it never did and just came off feeling like a job I paid into instead of got paid for.

Long review: I really didn't want to write this review but felt compelled to as the result was so far from the expectation. It feels like I am picking on my best friend's little sister. I SHOULD love this game. I love 4x games. I love space themed 4x the most. To this day, some of my fondest memories are endless summers spent playing Master of Orion or Sid Meyer's Alpha Centauri. If only Endless Space 2 could capture my heart like those endless summers.

The first few hours are indeed enchanting. I was absolutely stunned by the gorgeous presentation of the game which seemingly graces every part of it down to the smallest detail. The races all have a different feel and different flavor mechanics. They also have their own story and quest line. The UI is just as close to perfection as I can imagine. The menus and management screens are so fluid and easy to navigate that old school 4x players may actually have a harder time adjusting than a brand new player to the genre. The graphics are beautiful. There are just enough resources, both "strategic" and "luxury" for them to feel like they matter but not so many for a player to get lost in. The Sophons have so much character and are so fun to interact with I always dupe them for the AI to play if I play them as well. The Lumeris leader owns my heart. So much is so right in Endless Space 2 but for me at least, it just doesn't last.

The polish started wearing off quickly. The first hints of this were with the exploration. It's hard to pin down but the wonder of discovery just evaporates. One anomaly feels much the same as another after a short amount of time. Another nebula or black hole is discovered, cataloged and quickly forgotten. Their impact or possibility on your game feeling shallow and meaningless. Once that irritation came and went I soured on some other issues. The sound, though technically fine just feels so flat and soulless. The music score is bland and repetitive. The effects utilitarian. This clashes with the excellent graphics. After the first few space battle scenes I toggled off the watch button and never looked back. The ground battles aren't even worth watching once except as a learning experience to never bother watching them again. The research starts feeling tiresome and predictable way too soon. After a half day of play I was tired of it and realized just how static it is for every game with only slight alterations depending on race or map. The victory conditions never feel immediately concerning. Perhaps what bothered me the most is I never once felt like I had a secret weapon, strategy, or tactic. Don't get me wrong, I had effective moments in both military and non-military aspects of the game but none of them ever wowed me. Ever.

In the end, for me at least, Endless Space 2 feels like a slightly more complicated Talisman game. It feels more like I am playing a digital board game than a proper 4x video game. That may not be a fair judgment but that's how it feels playing it. To me, Endless Space 2 is almost the exact opposite of Distant Worlds Universe: Beautiful, easy to get along with, easy to learn, and tediously boring.

As I said, I didn't enjoy reviewing this. So much about Endless Space 2 feels so good I just want to give a thumbs up to Amplitude for no other reason than encouragment but at the same time, after a week I don't feel any need to play it anymore and instead have a rekindled interest in my other 4x games.

So I decided to pick Endless Space 2 up in a recent sale, having really enjoyed the original.
I'd heard it had some issues and the devs were tending to it, but I thought it had been long enough as well that anything serious would be done.

Unfortunately I feel I was wrong in that hope.


So to start with the positives, Endless Space 2 feels as if a AAA company took ES1 and spent 2 years focusing on nothing but pure immersion. The game looks spectacular and the old narrative feeling is back.
Gameplay is relatively similar, though combat has been overhauled to some extent, with tactics being a once-a-battle thing now and it's decided before-hand not mid-battle.

The new combat is great by the way. The new land battles helps add to the flavor of the game, though sometimes I feel it doesn't make sense, such as when you want 30% of your army to be aircraft and you end up with loadouts you can't control where you might have 80 infantry, 30 tanks, and 2 aircraft.

From there we get onto some more disappointing points.

Firstly is performance. A game of Endless Space 2 is meant to run about 300 turns. If you play on slow, about 450 turns. But with my own specs of an i7-6700K, GTX 1080Ti and 16GB RAM, on top of having the game on an SSD, performance becomes sloppy inside 150 turns with ease. Battles start having random stutters and turns themselves slow down to some extent (Though I will give it credit for not being anywhere near as bad as Firaxis' trademark mega waits for Civilization turns)

We come to the two points now that I feel are the most critical in why I'm unfortunately disappointed so far:

1: The AI.
The AI feels incomplete. It mocks you every few turns like clockwork, simply tells you what it's going to do in a few turns (Like going to war), and its ability to build up its own empire is...strange at best.
The AI manages to expand rapidly at the start. I'm not the most experienced player but on normal I definitely felt the AI outpaced me by miles in the early-game periods. However that quickly changes as the AI gets bogged down over nothing and thus doing nothing. An AI can go to war with you and simply never try to attack, or when they do it's for the one system they seem to want and that's it, or they just want to abduct people for 30 turns.

From a diplomacy standpoint the AI is full-on idiotic. An AI declares war on you due to having the opportunistic trait and you are at war already, but you take 10 systems off of them and they will still simply refuse peacedeals point blank when the war is about to wipe them out the game. It simply feels like the AI barely takes anything into account, and ultimately after about 100+ turns I feel like the AI just falls apart entirely.
On a side note, if you get an AI ally, they will go to war without saying anything, then insult you for not helping every 3-4 turns, but there is simply no way to be asked to join a war or offer, you just have to know who they are at war with and do it manually. It might work but it's impractical in this day-in-age for a 4X game.


For the second point, we have UI and events.

I enjoy the atmosphere of Endless Space and I like the overall gameplay, but I swear that I have *never* seen a game with such blatant disregard for player input as Endless Space 2. The standard 4X events are practically full-screen on this game, and they will pop up almost randomly. Sometimes a start-of-turn event will popup 10-15 seconds after you are navigating some other menu. There is no coherency between menu panels because you will get an option to go see something, click it, and then it has simply replaced it with a new event to go see something else.  

Ultimately the events could outspam a dedicated spambot on reddit, with the game basically mandating that you try and manually turn off as many of the more pointless events as possible so you can feel sane when you click end-turn.



Update: So I've put a bit more time in, another 5-6 hours and found a few new issues. Some petty, some outrageous:

- The AI shutting its borders whilst you blockade them appears to despawn your blockading fleet from the game, but it keeps it in your lists and keeps charging you for it, you effectively lose the ships permanently. If this is otherwise, the game is not saying. (So I just lost about 1.2M dust worth of ship value and it's now draining 9,000 manpower a turn at random. Seems to be 100% broken)
-AI's late-game tactics appear to be trying to spam one planet with 5-6 bad fleets so that they can keep it permanently guarded and keep getting land battles in, even though they cannot win a single space battle
-Even trying to work out what treaties you have with everyone is a serious hassle. You might as well write them down because unless you are allowed to cancel it right now, you can't see what treaties are there.
-Performance has become cripplingly low in terms of turn timers and just trying to get battles to load, this is by turn 200-210 on a 300-turn game on a large map with 8 players...
-Nothing and I mean *nothing* scales properly in this game. I make 9,000 dust a turn but the AI offers me peace and 39 dust per turn. At the start of my latest game, with 3 systems in my empire, a minor system asked me to build 18 buildings in 15 turns...suffice to say that was impossible.
-Lastly, I won a supremacy game and it turned around and told me to go to the score screen, only to sit on the loading menu for 3 minutes and never load it at all.

End of Update


In summary, I want to reiterate that overall I do like the game. I feel the best way to describe Endless Space 2 is it feels like a AAA company made it, but it's as if they've never done anything even remotely similar to this game before. I enjoy the game for only as long as the events can be kept at bay (Which they often can't) and the AI stays competent(which again it often doesn't).

I'm going to have to say that even on sale, you might be disappointed with the state it is in, despite how visually appealing it is and how great the core gameplay itself still is too. I would check back and see if the devs have been able to alleviate at least the AI in the future.

After all the stuff I posted in the update section, I have to say this is an even greater disappointment than I thought. It's a shame because Endless Space 1 is great. You are better off just playing the original, as this sequel doesn't deserve to be in the same series.

This game has a lot of potential, minus a few minor issues.  That said it comes to a point where it becomes virtually unplayable due to an unaddressed bug which prevents you from ending the turn.  I do not play with any mods.   I have played about 9-10 games sofar, and this bug has occurred in all of my games bar none.  It sometimes gets to a point where every 2-3 turns cannot be ended.  The "solution" is to reload and end the turn but having to do so all the time just puts me off.

I certainly would not have thumbs down this game had it been new as it would mean you would expect them to fix this bug soon.  But this game has been out for years, and is thus supposed to be a refined product.  Further to this having done my research it seems that many others are facing this issue.  The fact that this game has been out for years and this issue is not fixed means a future fix is much less likely.

I have worked in the games industry as a programmer and can say that some bugs are harder to fix than others.  However I can state beyond a doubt to anyone reading this post that bugs that happen very often (thus that are easy to reproduce) are much easier to fix than those that do not.  And since they happen in all my games and that of many others that I have read online (for years apparently), this just displays poor support for a product that is supposed to be refined.

EDIT: I have found a workaround to this bug, hence the hours played since this review.  Re-closing all the dialogues on the right solves it.  

Unfortunately I still cannot recommend this game, at least for single play.  I am now playing on the next highest difficulty and the AI is about the worst I have seen in a strategy game.  Despite having overwhelmingly more resources than the player on higher difficulty settings, it wont do basic things like defending its systems (cities).  Unless the AI declare war on you early game (where they come in with pre-emptive stacks), they pose very little threat.  What this translates into is that mid to late game, you build an "army" fleet and simply walk into their systems (cities), take them over one by one often without the slightest resistence.  Other times they will fight back but with scattered fleets that are typically inferior to yours even though you have not updated yours in a while. Again this on super high difficulty settings.

The TLDR of this AI issue is that it makes the game virtually pointless and non challenging.  If you KNOW that you can simply take over the AI's systems at any time, particularly beyond early game, there is little point in even playing.  I have looked for AI mods but have fallen short, so I am playing what I believe will be my final games on this before wrapping it up for good.

The forums are full of people complaining about the AI with the typical response of "just play online" which is something that I don't want to do.  If you see yourself as willing to do so, by all means get this game.  But be prepared for some heavy RNG when it comes to starting locations - they can be pure bliss or just so disadvantageous that you will never have a fighting chance.  Thats my only other complaint about the game other than the AI and the obvious bug to which I had to personally find a workaround.  

TLDR; get this game only if you are willing to play online and are prepared for some heavy RNG when it comes to starting locations.  Remember to close the dialogues on the the right when the end turn freezes.

((Early Access Review))
Many early access games on Steam nowadays are either incomplete shells of projects that either take way too long to complete, are too broken to play, or will be released in a broken incomplete shape.

But not with Amplitude studios! This is an early access game that can be played and actually enjoyed as if it were a full release. And the full release is just around the corner, on May 19. The devs are very active with their updates and constantly acknowledging player feedback, which is wonderful business practice.
Yes there are some minor quirks and issues. Some surprisingly small bugs here and there. But the game is remarkably stable and fluid, I've rarely noticed those bugs and they rarely interrupt the game flow. Worst case scenario, saving and reloading will solve almost anything.

There is a solid amount of content and gameplay features. You currently have 7 major factions to choose from to build your space empire. And they are all very unique, each having their own gimmicks and strategies. And each can be played in multiple different styles. So if you're playing the currently popular Vodyani, you don't have to be constantly warmongering. You could play military victory and conquer the galaxy, but you can also pursue economic playstyles taking into consideration their faction mechanics.
Later on, they will add custom factions, which is my favorite feature in most 4X games!

There is a staggering number of minor factions as well, which is a new feature not present in Endless Space 1. There are entire strategies and empire bonuses just related to the minor factions ALONE. And yes, they also affect your political system in their own way. (That's right, there's a POLITICS mechanic in this game). They also have their own population units each with different yields and effects.

The galaxies generated are so different from one another with so many variables, that you will never feel deja vu. Every match is extremely different from the other. Very few strategy games can accomplish such variability and variety in the early game.

And if you're worried about the mid and late game (which is where most 4X strategy games might suffer), Endless Space 2 has the cure!
As you progress through the tech tree, you continue to unlock more empire features. You don't need them all though. So for example if you're playing with the warmongering Cravers, you don't really need to unlock the Resource market. It's optional, but there's probably other better stuff you need to research to improve your attack ships. Meanwhile, If you're playing the Lumeris trader faction, the resource market would be more useful to you than ship ugrades or Influence projects. So on and so forth...

So you will never get bored with Empire management. There are always new things to do in the mid game. New features to unlock and new strategic options you could take. The late game can be made more involving with future updates like major galaxy events. Terraforming planets is also currenrly available. And if you still get bored, big wars are always just a few clicks away!
I won't say much about combat, because that is clearly not the main focus of this game, even for military factions. BUT, even then, the combat is still an enjoyable experience. And once again there are lots of variables to consider in ship building, too many to mention here. The adviser will even explain certain features that are unique to each faction. The Amplitude community is, as usual, always very helpful, friendly and open to dialogue. You will never feel any hostility in this community.

The music is awesome and fits the atmosphere perfectly. There's a youtube channel that has all the major faction tracks, and they are gorgeous!
If they sell the music for this game, I would not hesitate to buy it. It's relaxing, which makes it a good listen while driving to work.

Overall, if you liked Endless Space or any other Amplitude game, you will love this one. Plus Endless Space 2 is twice as good as the prequel even with all of its expansions. So ES2 will have even more awesome results in the future.
If you're new to space strategy or the Endless franchise, you might want to wait for full release. But I would still recommend this game to you.

After playing almost two matches, here is my review of an extremely promising yet still unfinished game. This title is in Early Access, which means that it won't be done until Amplitude say it is done. Promising a full release in approximately six months from now, they have big shoes to fill, but ultimately I believe they can deliver.

Pros:
+ Beautiful UI and Graphics for a 4X game.
+ Each of the four current factions are varied and interesting. (There will be 8 on release)
+ You really get a feel of managing an empire, especially with the political parties.
+ Combat is very fun assuming you accept it for what it is.
+ Added really fun exploration mechanics with probes and constellations as well as random rogue systems.
+ Kept the interesting tech tree style from Endless Legend, which really emphasizes choice if you want to keep up in technology.
+ Feels like a living galaxy with minor factions and all the events and quests.
+ Managing your political parties is fun and interesting, especially when outside events make it difficult for your favored party to stay dominant (I'm looking at you militarist party, stop dominating my senate when people declare war on me).
+ Outpost system feels realistic and contesting systems can be fun.

Fixes needed
- Camera in space battles is janky and often doesn't show interesting angles.
- Score Victory is sort of arbitrary and leads to short games.
- Incomplete Tech Tree. Only goes up to Era 3.
- So many different technologies to research in order to colonize different kinds of planets.
- Lack of luxury resources meaning advancing system levels are difficult in some games.
- Forced truces in a war can feel very unsatisfying in some situations. It's hard to keep up a war in this game, but when you can, it feels like forced truces really hinder the experience.
- Happiness system feels incomplete, would like some way to influence it like the tax system from Endless Space 1 or some other interactive system.
- Repairing ships is too expensive (this will be fixed).
- Other unfinished features.

Feature I'm missing the most since they're still working on it: Automation on star systems. I don't use it all the time, but come mid/late game sometimes I'd rather manage all the larger things than simply scrolling through every system. isn't a big deal in the current build, but I can't wait until they put that feature from ES1 and EL back in.

Overall: I recommend this game completely. Knowing Amplitude Studio's track record, I believe that once they get into gear, all of these problems will be addressed in some form. If you're looking for a complete game however, I would hold off for a few months or wait until the full release. While it is more interesting to play than ES and EL, it does currently lack features or contain unfinished features. I don't have a real con list until more things are added to the game. There are some downsides, but I don't feel like they're worth going that indepth about until closer to release, I do mention a few down below with some more indepth thoughts.

Exploration: I love the probes and constellations as well as random star systems sitting in the middle of no where with no space lanes connected to them. While it might be annoying to build scouts and stuff, I feel like this adds a really good feel towards a galaxy that is worth exploring. Probes able to explore planets for anamolies and resources is a nice touch too.

Expansion: Outposts feel a combination of really good and boring. I love the idea behind it, though waiting a bunch of turns is annoying. Outside of the waiting period, contesting a system by trying to finish your outpost before the enemy completes their's was interesting, though I have only experienced it once. I can imagine it being annoying for some people though. Colonizing planets can be annoying because you need to research tech for almost each planet type, though they make it a bit more satisfying by tying other bonuses to researching the planet tech. Sometimes being able to colonize a type of planet isn't the main reason you research that technology. I also don't think it's intended that you colonize every star system on the map, not until late game at least as it can get very difficult to manage everything.

Exploitation: There are a myriad of technologies to research in order to develop your star systems and your populations feel very dynamic for the most part. Political parties can rise and fall in an instant and influence a lot of things about your empire. Your ability to manage your population is huge in this game. Keeping your scientists in power is hard when trying to ally with a minor faction brings your pacifists into dominance, and tempering your population's militarist uprising is difficult when an enemy declares war on you. Keeping your favorite party in power to keep some needed laws is challenging and fun. Technologies to develop your star systems feel good for the most part and even researching the right technologies is difficult and rewarding. A lot about this game is managing short term vs long term and I feel like all these systems in concert bring an excellent feel to a game that few are able to implement well. I suspect with more polishing, this will get even more satisfying. Some people might not like the research system though, as you most likely won't unlock every technology in every era.

Extermination: Combat is overall very satisfying. I feel some work on ground battles is needed to make them feel a little better, but they feel pretty good, better than ES1 atleast. I really wonder how the reinforcement fleets will work out. One of ES1's biggest downfalls in combat was amassing large numbers of fleets felt really stale when you'd have 10 fleets all fighting. At that point it just turned into auto resolving everything and it seems like they might have something to address it coming in the future. Strategy helps a lot in this iteration and I feel the customization of ships is vastly better than ES1. I do wish there was more than three ways to move your fleet formations in though and maybe they'll address that in the future. Some people won't like the more hands off approach, but these aren't for a tactical master, these battles are for the strategist, who will meticulously plan out their victory from 10 turns earlier, who studied enemy ship designs in previous battles and who will choose the battle formations that fit their ship compositions and then watch the fruits of their labor engage in battle.

Keep in mind these are only my thoughts, some of what I consider great things, you might not. Thank you for reading.

While this game is truly the most gorgeous 4x game I've ever seen, stay away. Stay far away.

First off, the game often corrupts saved games. You may be able to play a game and even save it, however if you try to load that game you may be unable to. Your game may be corrupted and the game will lock up every time you try to load it. As 4x games tend to take more than one session to play, I'd consider this to be a gamebreaking bug. The game should never have gone retail without the ability to load a saved game, and we're long past it going retail.

The AI is quite poor when carrying out a war. At high difficulty levels the AI gets massive industry, science, and money bonuses. While this is standard fare for high difficulty modes on 4x games, all it means is that the AI will immediately begin producing vast quantities of really big ships. However the AI appears to be incapable of using them. You may be woefully outmatched by the AI with their fleets of dreadnoughts, but thats okay. The AI is happy to declare war on you at the drop of a hat, but seems unable to follow up with its declaration of war and actually attack. The end result is that the AI feels extremely passive. The entire game, even on maximum difficulty level, feels like a mop-up operation where the game has already been decided and you're already the victor, but you need to clean up the map anyways.

Another bug, though not gamebreaking is also quite annoying. The auto-build function does not work. Most 4x games have some sort of auto-build function. If you have a lot of settlements it can be a chore to manage them all. Auto-manage comes to the rescue. It should over time build all available improvements so a low priority settlement can take care of itself. The build order might not be ideal, but thats fine, you're only using it for the low priority ones. Unfortunately in Endless Space 2 this simple function does not work. The auto-build queue stops working and stops building improvements for no rhyme or reason. It just stops. You end up having to micro-manage every single star system every single turn. On large maps this can be quite a chore indeed.

Gameplay itself is almost entirely obfuscated. 4x games are really just spreadsheets with a lot of window dressing, but as part of that the player must have clear feedback. Players cannot be left in the dark as to why something happened, or what the result of a player decision are. Unfortunately Endless Space 2 gives close to zero player feedback in multiple areas;

* Diplomacy with AI players is baffling. The AI will routinely accuse you of making hostile gestures at them even when your fleet is orbiting your own homeworld. The AI may also accuse you of blockading their systems while your fleet is orbiting your own homeworld. There is often no indication as to why the AI suddenly hates you. You don't have to do anything and sometimes the AI gives you messages saying its hates you, sometimes the AI sends you messages saying it loves you. There's no feedback between cause and effect.

* Combat is mystifying. Weapons have long/medium/short engagement ranges. You can deploy at long/medium/short range, but so can your enemy. If you pick short range and they pick long range, at what range do your weapons actually engage at? Is one flotilla shooting at another a short range attack? Long range attack? There's no feedback, so all you can do is build lots of defenses, lots of weapons, and hope for the best. Expensive ships with all of the upgrades beat less expensive ships. The actual mechanics of combat are entirely unclear. 

* Icons aren't explained in tool tips. You may eventually figure out what luxury goods boost what stats, but this will require a great deal of trial and error. The tooltip will happily explain what something does, but it uses an icon to explain what the thing does. Unfortunately at no point is that icon explained, so you're left with a tooltip that may as well be in hieroglyphics.

Overall verdict:

Major game features are broken or poorly implemented. The ability to save/load a game successfully is dubious at best. AI is passive. Expect a lot of tedious micromanagement for no benefit. The game provides little to no feedback to player actions, leading to a lot of guesswork from the player.

But its a really, really, really pretty game. Its downright gorgeous.

Pick it up if its on sale, but wait until it hits $15 or so. It sure is pretty as an art project, but its not a good game.

This is far and away my go-to 4X game when I just want that 4X fantasy. The setting, the distinct mechanics of the different civs, the little story bits (not the random events which are kind of generic) for each civ "quest", all really just sell the universe to me. I only played Endless Space 1 once or twice before jumping into this, so it's hard to compare them, but it is a bit easier to parse than Endless Legend and while the city / system management is apples to oranges, I find the system management interesting and offering options while not being as messy as EL (and still way more interesting than Civ 5 or 6). 

The battles are probably a divisive thing - it's basically fleet vs. fleet, stat checks, although you can watch it play out if you like (once in a while it's nice to see ships go pew pew if you are warring). Whether you win or lose a battle comes from ship design, fleet management, and tactics cards which you pick 1 of at the start of the battle (these can have massive impacts on outcomes). But, since you're often dealing with multiple fleets across many systems across the span of a game, losing one fleet is not always that big a deal.

The expansions are generally good to me, although they seem to have poor reviews, I do think they perhaps feel expensive for what they add (one more unique civ and usually something gamewide for all civs / players). The Penumbra being the most unique in the game by quite a bit, a shadowy "hacker" race that doesn't colonize planets the way the others do. The ones added in Awakening and Supremacy aren't nearly as distinct but they are still interesting enough to play a bit differently than the other "basic" civs like Sophons and Empire. Supremacy adds probably the best "tall" civ for the game, although it's still a space 4X so you need some systems.

You've been playing this game for 41 hours now. You love it. Like Civilisation but set in space and with a crazy notion of adding role playing and decision branching story-like elements.

I know the above sentence doesn't quite make sense but bear with me, I will explain.  Firstly, let me say I love this game and personally think it's better than Civ4 and above, maybe even Civ 2!  Blasphemy I know, but this game blends the turn based strategy and micromanaging economy aspects of Civilisation but then adds in Role playing and deep story/lore too (a la Alpha Centauri).  But, it can be very daunting for anyone who isn't familiar to it.

For starters, you play as a space faring faction/civilisation and you have to manage your production, economy and military very similar to Civilisation.  Buildings will give you bonuses, improve defences or there are even wonders and faction wonders too.  You will need to colonise planets in a system by setting up outposts on a planet and also researching the ability to colonise new harsher planet types.  different planets give you different base stats to your people working them, and even race specific penalties or boosts.  For instance you might have a specific race that has a bonus on fertile planets, or you might have some bonuses on hot or cold planets.  You will have your starting race, but you will also have other races in your civilisation, each with their own bonuses/benefits etc.  Managing the amounts of these people and where they are is important.  With all that said, the economy can be quite daunting with trading or resources/luxury items and even a stock market and all the previous aspects to think about.  My advice is to look for some good guides or just play a game and see how it goes.

Unlike civilisation exploration is a little more straight forward, being that you navigate stars via corridors/lanes (think slipstreams or warp gates) and you discover systems and travel within constellations until you find a way to travel outside of these limits.  You have units in fleets that can fight enemies and even cold war like enemies if you or they stray too close.  You can customise your units and part of the strategy is about countering what the enemy will or can throw at you whilst also lobbing stuff back they can't counter.

What sets this game apart is the fact your factions can drastically change your play style.  For instance, you might play as the Hissho, who are war like and 'buy/build' things using a currency you get by fighting.  Or on the opposite end of the spectrum you might play as the Unfallen, who are peaceful tree-like race that just want to 'peacefully' extend their roots to other systems, even other factions systems who get a bonus to their economy so it's a win win right?  Underpinning this is a rich story about the galaxies history and this mysterious dust currency as well as backgrounds for all factions and minor factions.  I love this aspect of the game.  To build upon this you have 'story' which involves quests and your specific faction will also have story quests that can give you rewards or hamper you randomly.

I like this game but to be honest I play solo and geek out to the beautiful artwork and story elements to the game.  I know it's not for everyone, but if you fall into that niche of liking turn based strategy, role playing and story then this game is worth a shot.

This used to be one of my favorite games... then the devs released three expansions in a row that, over time, changed the game mechanics in ways that have made certain factions completely unplayable and destroyed much of the 'fun' in the game.

The first expansion (Vaulters) was good. The Vaulters had an interesting game mechanic and no changes had to be made to the other factions in order for the game to function as a whole. That's not to say that everything was perfect, but the game was still fun no matter which faction you chose to play.

The second expansion (Supremacy) added the Hissho faction and behemoths. The faction was interesting but behemoths are just bad in every way. You get the same boring behemoths for every faction, they don't add any interesting gameplay elements, and changes started being made to the other factions to balance them for the new mechanics... and the devs began stripping 'fun' elements out of the game in a half-assed attempt to balance everything.

The third expansion (Penumbra) added the hacking feature and the Umbral Choir faction, an invisible enemy that required all the existing factions to be changed in order to make them work. Aside from the fact that hacking is simply uninteresting, battle elements that were fun had to be stripped from the game in order to accommodate an environment where cyber attacks could be viable. Almost every faction's ships were modified in little ways that began destroying the viability of several original factions. The Umbral Choir faction was also boring.

The last expansion (Awakening) introduced the Nakalim faction with yet more uninteresting game mechanics. More changes were made to other factions and the result is a game that no longer works well. In the end, if you do not want to play the game with the last three expansions, game mechanics that were necessary for those expansions to work are now embedded in the game, affecting it even though the reasons for those changes aren't relevant if you don't own (or choose not to play with) one or more of the expansions. The result is a game that has morphed over time into something that is no longer fun to play and I can't recommend it.

[b][i]Endless Space 2[/i][/b], does a great job of making governance feel like an epic accomplishment. Every technology and development choice you can make feels incredibly useful and powerful. You can see your empire improving turn-by-turn.

The game is very flexible like that, in that there are truly multiple ways to play and win, and not all of it is under your control. Sometimes even if you want peace, too many people are around you initially, or you want war but the star lanes to travel are terribly long and its just not possible.

Graphically the game is good. Some of the effects are a little cheap, like ground battles, but others, like the ship battles you can watch, look really good. Sound is good as well, with some decent voice acting.

With a much improved tutorial advisor, fantastic graphics, and race specific storylines, [b][i]Endless Space 2[/i][/b] is a galactic adventure worth having. The races are all unique and challenging to master, but well worth the effort and you will easily find yourself attached to your favorites. There is still room for the tutorial to explain more about the game and its mechanics however, and it wouldn’t hurt to allow proper command of your fleets in space combat as opposed to watching them carry out a single order. Endless Space 2 is a must for fans of 4X and strategy titles.

[b][i]Endless Space 2[/i][/b] is one of the strongest 4X games in recent memory, even if it's not the deepest.

Well. This review is mildly overdue, but heck, I'm still gonna write it regardless.
A very detailed and well-made 4X TBS that was my first experience in the genre and a mighty good one at that! After watching Sseth's video I was so intrigued by what he had to say that I decided to buy the whole package immediately and never had any regrets for doing it for the full price.
Disclaimer: if you are unfamiliar with the genre (like I was), your first experience is either going to give you extreme headaches from enormous amount of information contained in the gameplay, or if you're more of gradual learner- just take from 20 to 40hrs respectively. That's just the way it is.
*)Despite the length of the review, I will only list the Basics and some very easy to understand concepts so you can form an light and somewhat unbiased opinion about the game. No one wants to read piles of descriptions and calculations about advanced gameplay unless it's a gaming YouTube channel or a specific guide /article. 
Now onto the objective (and sometimes- subjective):

1)General gameplay- is generally (!!!) the same for all 12 major factions of the game, with several strategical routes available, each one corresponding to the victory types that are currently in the game. Simplified: want to win economically or scientifically: farm dust (main in game value) or tech upgrades respectively; or if you're an avid follower of Teddy Roosevelt's famous saying- just whack all your opponents instead; etc... Besides the grinding system of FIDSI -(main components of the game's economy: Food, Industry, Dust, Science, Influence), the details of your path to victory, besides the route you wish to take are mostly dependent on the unique gameplay variations of each major faction and can be classified like this:
a)Minor stuff- like easy to learn ''grind'' perks for Sophons, United Empire, Horatio, Vaulters and Lumeris;
b)More complex stuff- like Hissho, Riftborn, Nakalim, and Cravers;
c)And really challenging stuff- like Unfallen, Umbral Choir and Vodyani.
*)Difficulties are subjective as are most of the opinions, and some people might disagree with my ranking, but it's mine for a reason.

Some side notes before the 2nd part:
General gameplay is divided into several sections, but all of it is essentially decision making of different kind. Construction- what to build; Heroes management- who to hire&customize; Politics- which determine the main course of your empire; Science- what to research; Military- whom to whack, etc... Despite the seemingly complex system, there are only three gameplay phases: the Galaxy map which gives you an overview of everything from planets to fleets and where you will be making almost all of your decisions; Combat Sim cutscenes (because everything regarding combat is done during map phase); and specific windows: Diplomacy (self explanatory), Politics, Tech and Military ("shipyard" which upgrade your ship designs, and "barracks" - which offer different additional upgrades aside from tech ones). 

There is a LOT of lore&information in this game. Most of it is told through cinematics (two per faction, plus three Academy quest line endings), lengthy written "briefings" before each faction specific mission, and many, less lengthy for what it's worth, descriptions for neutral quests and almost every action and decision you're about to make during gameplay.

2)Onto the second most interesting subject- Major Factions themselves. They are all unique, with their own set of strengths&weaknesses, and general gameplay "preferences". I will not be telling anything about their gameplay because it will ruin your precious first time experience of reading through piles of texts so instead- I will be "ranking" in a specific way: Difficulty (of gameplay*), Quality (how interesting and engaging the gameplay is), Visuals&Aesthetics, Lore; also some short side notes below:
a)The Sophons- Easy; B+; A-; A.
Fairly vanilla faction with a straight way towards Science victory. 
b)The Cravers- Easy+; B-; A; A.
Militaristic faction. Very one dimensional gameplay. You will either like them, or not.
c)The Lumeris- Easy+; A-; B+; B+.
Hybrid faction. The Economy victory is the easiest, but can do military or science as well.
d)The Riftborn- Medium; A; A-; A.
Hybrid faction. The Science and Wonder victory are the easiest, but can do military too.
e)The Unfallen- Hard+; A; A; A.
The hardest faction in the game to play good. Hybrid with either Conquest or Wonder victory being the only solid choices, but can branch out (pun intended) towards science.
f)The Vodyani- Hard-; A; S; A.
Very tough to play properly Hybrid faction with the strongest late game. Due to faction specific mechanics can do all of the victory types. 
g)The United Empire- Easy; B+; A+; A-.
Very beginner friendly Hybrid faction. Basically- grind gameplay. Multiple victory types feasible most prominent being Conquest, Science or Wonder.
h)The Horatio- Easy; A-; A; A-.
Beginner friendly Hybrid faction. The only gameplay difficulty is proper splicing order. Easiest victory types are Science and Wonder.
DLC Factions:
i)The Vaulters- Easy+; A; A+; A+.
Beginner friendly Hybrid faction. Certain faction gameplay specifics make it nigh impossible to do anything except Science and Wonder.
j)The Hissho- Medium+; A; S; A+.
Despite what some people might say- not beginner friendly Hybrid faction. Anything except Wonder or military related is very hard.
k)The Umbral Choir- Hard; B+; A-; A+.
NOT beginner friendly faction. I do not like their gameplay nor have I played them alot, but Science is still the easiest option.
l)The Nakalim- Medium; A; B+; A+.
Not very easy hybrid faction. Faction specific trait makes it nigh impossible to win a Science victory but everything else (except Economic) is feasible.
*)Custom factions- will be your bread and butter after getting bored with the major ones. You can create anything you like in this game, including changing your starting hero to suit your needs. 
*)The are a ton of minor factions in this game, which act mostly as cattle to be conquered or diplomatically coerced to join your empire. Pirates act as a gameplay obstacle unless you can reason with them (Vaulters DLC).  The Academy faction (Awakening) is NOT a problem, despite what people say. You can tweak their difficulty before starting the game and they aren't really as obnoxious as folks tell.

Last side note: Graphics are bonkers. Everything looks as crisp and fresh as an AAA title. Voice acting is S tier for all the factions. Cinematics aren't particularly great, but all of them are very immersive and add to the quality of this game. The music  is FANTASTING. Almost all faction themes and ambient tracks sound really refreshing and add some needed immersion to the gameplay. Objectively best faction tracks are going to be: Unfallen (with clarinet, bass clarinet and harp solos), The Vaulters (with cello and viola solos), The Hissho (with winds and percussion), The Vodyani (solo alto/soprano) and United Empire (huge ass choir). The whole soundtrack by FlyByNo is available on the Internet and it's of great quality.

Overall, the game is great. It's not as balanced as you would expect it to be, but it has a lot of soul in it and I was kept very busy and interested for at least 400hrs. The sheer amount of gameplay mechanics including empire management, military management, planetary exploration/expansion, and I haven't even mentioned multiplayer which has some funny shenanigans too... Plus also, hey, there are still amphibious mommy milkers to look upon...                                                                                                                                              9/10.

Endless Space 2: Dust Boogaloo

There's a TL;DR at the bottom but I'd really appreciate it if you read it :)

If you're a fan of strategy games in the same vein as Civ or EU, pick this up.
If you're a fan of sci-fi, from ship customization to crazy technology trees, pick this up.
Or if you're a fan of fantastically written lore with an amazing attention to detail that leaves you feeling like you're truly in command of an entire galactic civilization,
Pick.
This.
Up.

Now, for less raving about my love for this game and more specifics on the pros and cons:

Endless Space 2 categorizes itself as a 4x strategy game, similar to those named above. You take turns building improvements to your systems, moving ships to new systems, and colonizing new planets, all while trying to work towards one of the many paths to victory. What sets ES2 from it's competition is the use of factions and an intriguing quest system, both of which give you a higher purpose than just "winning the game".

The factions of ES2 vary greatly in mechanics as well as appearance. Examples include the Cravers, a bug-cyborg-hatred hybrid bent on enslaving the galaxy and draining every planet of it's resources, the Vodyani, a race of immortal vampire zealots kept immortal in suits powered by the essence of other living creatures, and the Unfallen, a race of tree people who will not hesitate to extend their vines and "peacefully" take all your stuff. In case that didn't win you over, I suggest looking up the playable races as well as the "minor factions" that you will encounter and befriend/annihilate/subjugate along your journey to total galactic domination. 

However, the flavor of each of the playable races is burned into their playstyle so well that each has a distinct feel to playing them. The Vodyani, for instance, are on a permanent crusade for their religion surrounding the "endless", a precursor race. This endless search has led to them living on massive base ships called "Arks". This makes them highly mobile and threatening early on, but also allows them to ditch whatever system they colonize for better ones as soon as they're spotted. This, combined with their religious ability allowing them to invade without declaring war, makes it easy to give your enemies the SUCC on their best systems, draining them out before taking them for yourself. 

Each playable race also has a storyline quest it can follow, giving you further background and some choice about which direction you take your race. Your decisions even have an impact on how the quest turns out, so it gives additional flavor and meaning to what are just normal turns in other 4x games.

Now, as much as I love the game, it does have it's issues (although I would say that they aren't nearly as bad as some make them out to be). Even then, balance issues only become a problem if you download the latest large DLC pack: Supremacy. As of making this review, the new class of ship "Behemoth" has raised some issues with the later stages of the game. In particular, the model that allows for long range destruction of other players' systems has caused me some frustration. When an enemy player targets one of your systems with the ship, there are no notifications or anything of the sort, besides the beam which can be visible from zooming out of the map. You can build defenses against the beams, but these are largely a preventative measure, and you're already screwed if you try to build one once firing has started. However, the Behemoths can be turned off in settings, so this isn't even an issue if you don't want it to be. Besides, Games2Gether is fairly good at rolling out updates and balance changes so I'm sure it won't be around long.

------------------------------------------------TL;DR------------------------------------------------

In conclusion, I love this game. It's one of my favorite strategy games I've picked up, and I'm still incredibly addicted. If you want a great "one more turn" game with great flavor and lore, don't hesitate to pick this up.
